courses.title: General Surgery and Trauma
courses.description: Surgical principles, the acute abdomen, hernias, gastrointestinal and hepatobiliary surgery, breast and thyroid surgery, and management of trauma.

topics.title: Surgical Principles and Wound Care
topics.summary: Wound healing, surgical site infection, fluids and nutrition, and the WHO safe surgery checklist.

material.heading: Wounds and infection
material.body: Wound healing phases: haemostasis, inflammation (days 1–4), proliferation (granulation tissue, days 4–21) and remodelling (weeks to a year). Healing by primary intention (sutured clean wounds), secondary intention (open wounds filling with granulation — abscess cavities, contaminated wounds) and delayed primary closure (contaminated wounds closed after 3–5 days). Factors impairing healing: infection, poor blood supply, diabetes, malnutrition, steroids, smoking, anaemia and radiotherapy. Keloids are more common in people of African descent. Wound classes: clean, clean-contaminated, contaminated and dirty — guiding antibiotic prophylaxis (a single dose within 60 minutes before incision). Surgical site infection prevention: skin preparation (chlorhexidine–alcohol), avoid shaving (clip if needed), normothermia, glucose control and sterile technique. Abscesses need incision and drainage. Tetanus prophylaxis is essential for traumatic wounds. Necrotising fasciitis (pain out of proportion, crepitus, rapid spread) is a surgical emergency requiring radical debridement.

material.heading: Perioperative care and safety
material.body: Preoperative preparation includes assessment, consent, optimising comorbidities (anaemia, diabetes, hypertension), fasting, VTE risk assessment, and blood availability. Fluid management: replace deficits, maintain (about 25–30 mL/kg/day), and replace ongoing losses (vomiting — hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis in gastric outlet obstruction; fistula and NG losses). Nutrition: enteral feeding is preferred when the gut works; parenteral nutrition when not; refeeding syndrome (hypophosphataemia) in malnourished patients. The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist (sign in, time out, sign out) reduces complications and deaths. Access to safe surgery is limited in Nigeria (Lancet Commission on Global Surgery — 5 billion people lack access; target ≥ 20 surgeons, anaesthetists and obstetricians per 100,000). Common surgical diseases in Nigeria include hernias, typhoid perforation, appendicitis, trauma, breast and colorectal cancer, and complications of delayed presentation.
keyPoints: WHO checklist: sign in, time out, sign out

topics.title: The Acute Abdomen
topics.summary: Appendicitis, peritonitis, typhoid perforation, intestinal obstruction and acute pancreatitis.

material.heading: Inflammation and perforation
material.body: Acute appendicitis: periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa, anorexia, nausea, fever, tenderness at McBurney's point, rebound tenderness, Rovsing's sign; scoring (Alvarado) and ultrasound aid diagnosis; treat with appendicectomy (open or laparoscopic) and antibiotics; complications — perforation, abscess, appendix mass (conservative initially). Generalised peritonitis (board-like rigidity, guarding, absent bowel sounds, sepsis): causes in Nigeria include typhoid ileal perforation (young people, after 2–3 weeks of fever — resuscitate, antibiotics, laparotomy with repair or resection; high morbidity and mortality), perforated peptic ulcer (air under the diaphragm on erect chest X-ray; omental patch repair) and ruptured appendix. Acute pancreatitis (gallstones, alcohol): epigastric pain radiating to the back, raised amylase/lipase (> 3 times normal); supportive management with fluids, analgesia and nutrition; severity by Glasgow or Ranson criteria. Acute cholecystitis: RUQ pain, fever, Murphy's sign; antibiotics and cholecystectomy.

material.heading: Intestinal obstruction
material.body: Features: colicky abdominal pain, vomiting (early in proximal obstruction), abdominal distension and absolute constipation (early in distal obstruction); high-pitched bowel sounds; X-ray shows dilated loops with air–fluid levels (small bowel: central, valvulae conniventes crossing the whole width; large bowel: peripheral, haustra). Causes in Nigeria: adhesions (previous surgery), obstructed/strangulated hernias (common due to late presentation), sigmoid volvulus (common in northern Nigeria — 'coffee bean' sign; endoscopic decompression then elective resection or emergency sigmoidectomy), intussusception (infants — red-currant jelly stools, sausage-shaped mass; ultrasound 'target sign'; air or hydrostatic reduction), tumours (colorectal cancer), and Ascaris bolus in children. Management: 'drip and suck' (IV fluids, NG decompression), correct electrolytes, catheter and fluid balance, and surgery for strangulation (fever, tachycardia, constant pain, peritonism, raised lactate) or failure of conservative treatment.

topics.title: Hernias, Hepatobiliary and Colorectal Surgery
topics.summary: Groin hernias, gallstone disease, obstructive jaundice, colorectal cancer and anorectal conditions.

material.heading: Hernias and hepatobiliary
material.body: Inguinal hernias (most common, mainly in men; indirect — through the deep ring, lateral to inferior epigastric vessels, may reach the scrotum; direct — through Hesselbach's triangle, medial) are very common in Nigeria and often present late, obstructed or strangulated. Femoral hernias (women; below and lateral to the pubic tubercle) have a high risk of strangulation. Repair: Lichtenstein tension-free mesh repair (low-cost mosquito net mesh has been used safely in Africa). Umbilical hernias in children often close spontaneously by 4–5 years. Gallstone disease (increasing in Nigeria): biliary colic, cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis (obstructive jaundice), cholangitis (Charcot's triad — fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) and gallstone pancreatitis; laparoscopic cholecystectomy; ERCP for duct stones. Obstructive jaundice: causes include stones, carcinoma of the pancreatic head (Courvoisier's law — palpable gallbladder with painless jaundice unlikely to be stones), cholangiocarcinoma; ultrasound shows dilated ducts. Hepatocellular carcinoma and amoebic liver abscess (aspirate if large) are important in Nigeria.
keyPoints: Indirect: lateral to inferior epigastric vessels

material.heading: Colorectal and anorectal
material.body: Colorectal cancer is rising in Nigeria and often affects younger adults with late presentation (rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, iron-deficiency anaemia, abdominal mass, obstruction); digital rectal examination, colonoscopy and biopsy, CT staging, CEA; treatment is surgical resection (right hemicolectomy, anterior resection, abdominoperineal resection) with chemotherapy/radiotherapy; staging by TNM/Dukes. Anorectal conditions: haemorrhoids (painless bright red bleeding; grades I–IV; high-fibre diet, banding, haemorrhoidectomy), anal fissure (painful defecation, posterior midline; topical GTN or diltiazem, lateral internal sphincterotomy), perianal abscess (incision and drainage), fistula-in-ano (Goodsall's rule; fistulotomy or seton), and pilonidal sinus. Hirschsprung disease (absent ganglion cells — delayed passage of meconium in neonates) and anorectal malformations are paediatric surgical conditions.

topics.title: Breast, Thyroid and Surgical Oncology
topics.summary: Breast lumps and breast cancer, thyroid nodules and goitre surgery, and principles of cancer surgery.

material.heading: Breast
material.body: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in Nigerian women, often presenting at a young age and advanced stage (large masses, skin involvement — peau d'orange, ulceration, axillary nodes), with a high proportion of triple-negative tumours. Triple assessment of any breast lump: clinical examination, imaging (ultrasound under 35 years, mammography over 35) and tissue diagnosis (core needle biopsy or FNAC). Benign conditions: fibroadenoma (young women, mobile 'breast mouse'), fibrocystic changes, breast abscess (lactating women — drainage), and phyllodes tumour. Treatment of cancer: surgery (mastectomy — modified radical — or breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy; axillary surgery), chemotherapy (neoadjuvant for locally advanced), endocrine therapy (tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors for ER-positive), HER2-targeted therapy (trastuzumab) and palliative care. Breast awareness and clinical breast examination promote earlier detection.

material.heading: Thyroid and oncology principles
material.body: Goitre (simple, multinodular — common in iodine-deficient areas) and solitary thyroid nodules are evaluated by thyroid function tests, ultrasound and FNAC (Bethesda category). Indications for thyroidectomy: suspicion of malignancy, compressive symptoms (dyspnoea, dysphagia, retrosternal extension), thyrotoxicosis not controlled medically, and cosmesis. Thyroid cancers: papillary (commonest, lymphatic spread, good prognosis), follicular (haematogenous spread; more common in iodine-deficient areas), medullary (calcitonin; MEN2), and anaplastic (elderly, very aggressive). Complications of thyroidectomy: haemorrhage (neck haematoma causing airway compression — open the wound immediately), recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (hoarseness), hypocalcaemia (parathyroid damage — perioral tingling, Chvostek and Trousseau signs) and thyroid storm. Principles of surgical oncology: diagnosis by biopsy, staging (TNM), multidisciplinary team planning, curative resection with clear margins and lymphadenectomy, or palliative surgery (relieve obstruction, bleeding, pain).

topics.title: Trauma and Burns
topics.summary: ATLS approach, abdominal and chest trauma, head injury, and burn management.

material.heading: Trauma
material.body: Road traffic injuries, falls, gunshots and assaults make trauma a leading cause of death in young Nigerians; prehospital care is limited. The ATLS approach: primary survey (<C>ABCDE) with simultaneous resuscitation, adjuncts (FAST, chest and pelvic X-rays), secondary survey, and definitive care. Chest trauma: tension pneumothorax (needle decompression), open pneumothorax, massive haemothorax (> 1,500 mL on chest drain insertion — thoracotomy), flail chest and cardiac tamponade (Beck's triad — hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds; pericardiocentesis). Most chest injuries are managed with a chest drain alone. Abdominal trauma: blunt (spleen and liver most commonly injured) or penetrating; haemodynamically unstable patients with positive FAST need laparotomy; stable patients may have CT and non-operative management. Head injury: GCS assessment, prevent secondary brain injury (hypoxia, hypotension), CT scan, and neurosurgery for extradural or subdural haematoma. Damage control surgery limits operating time in physiologically deranged patients (the lethal triad — hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy).
keyPoints: Spleen and liver commonest in blunt trauma

material.heading: Burns
material.body: Burns in Nigeria commonly result from flames (kerosene, gas cylinders, petrol tanker explosions and fuel scooping), scalds in children and electrical injuries. Assessment: airway (inhalational injury — facial burns, singed nasal hair, hoarseness, carbonaceous sputum — early intubation), total body surface area (rule of nines in adults — head 9%, each arm 9%, front and back of trunk 18% each, each leg 18%, perineum 1%; palm method ~1%; Lund–Browder in children), and depth (superficial, superficial partial-thickness — blisters, painful; deep partial; full-thickness — leathery, painless). Fluid resuscitation for burns > 15% TBSA in adults (> 10% children) using the Parkland formula: 4 mL × weight (kg) × %TBSA of Ringer's lactate in 24 hours, half in the first 8 hours from the time of burn; titrate to urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h (1 mL/kg/h in children). Escharotomy for circumferential full-thickness burns; wound care, analgesia, nutrition, tetanus prophylaxis, infection control, early excision and grafting, and rehabilitation to prevent contractures.
